title: The resurrection of the body (CCC 988–1004)
hookLine: Catholics believe the whole person, body too, will be raised

lines: A BIRD OUT OF A CAGE?
cards: A bird flies out of an open cage, and the cage is left on the floor. A coat is shrugged off at the door and left on the hook.

People sometimes reach for those pictures when they talk about death: the soul goes free, the body stays behind. But in the Apostles' Creed, just before the last line, Christians say something stranger and more physical.
Not only the survival of the soul. Something about bodies: hands, faces, the scar on your knee. The Catholic Church says the coat isn't thrown away.

teach.b: In English the Creed ends: the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting. The Latin is even blunter: carnis resurrectionem, the resurrection of the flesh. Why the body?
The Catechism says a human being is one: body and soul together, not a soul trapped in a body. So salvation, in Catholic teaching, isn't escape from the body. It's the whole person, raised.
The early writer Tertullian made a Latin pun: caro salutis est cardo. The flesh is the hinge of salvation. Remember cardo, the hinge, from the four virtues?
Catholics say God took flesh, was raised in the flesh, and will raise ours. What kind of body? Not a corpse stitched back together.
Paul compares it to a seed and the plant it becomes: the same life, utterly changed.

teach.h: SOWN IN CORRUPTION, RISEN IN INCORRUPTION.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "It is sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption."

The Catechism says the dead will rise with their own bodies, the ones they have now, but changed, like Christ's glorious body, no longer able to die. How exactly, it says, goes beyond human imagination and understanding.
When: on the last day, when Christ returns. And if the body has a future, it isn't disposable. Paul says "your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost."
So Catholics are asked to respect their own bodies and everyone else's: the sick body, the aging body, the body in the grave.

how: Catholics profess the resurrection of the body in the Creed, bury their dead or reverently inter their ashes in consecrated places rather than scattering them, and honor the body in funeral rites as one day to be raised.

o: a dead body brought back to its old life
the soul set free when the body is left behind
the whole person, body too, raised and changed

p: the flesh is the hinge of salvation

s: Catholics believe only the soul lives on, and the body is left behind
the Creed professes the resurrection of the body: the whole person raised.
the Catechism says we'll rise with our own bodies, transformed
changed like Christ's glorious body, and no longer able to die.

games.q: the Corinthians ask Paul: how are the dead raised, and with what kind of body? what picture does he use?
o: a seed sown in the ground and the plant it becomes.
a soul that leaves its body like a coat.
games.why: a seed and its plant: the same life, utterly changed. sown in corruption, risen in incorruption.

practice: Start at your feet, which have carried you everywhere, and thank them; then your hands that have held people, your lungs filling right now without being asked, your heart beating since before you were born.
Notice any part that hurts, or that you've been unkind to in your head, and thank that part too. If you pray, you can thank God for the body you've been given.

wordCard.voice: Carnis resurrectionem, the Creed's Latin for the resurrection of the flesh: the whole person, body too, raised and transformed like Christ. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the Apostles' Creed: the resurrection of the flesh.

carryVoice: Your line: the body too. The week ran from Mary through the last things, death, judgment, purgatory, hell, heaven, and now the body too. Day three hundred twenty-nine: a week, done.
